title: Hadith commentary
hookLine: scholars like Ibn Hajar wrote vast commentaries

cards: How much can be said about one sentence? Not a summary of it. An explanation.
What each word means. Who carried it, and from whom. How another version words it.
What scholars drew from it, and where they parted ways. Put all that under a line you could say in one breath, and it runs on for pages.
The scholar Ibn Hajar wrote one of these on the whole of Sahih al-Bukhari, a vast work, saying by saying. That surrounding writing has a name. Today: sharh.

teach.b: Sharh means explanation: a commentary written on a hadith collection, one report at a time. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani wrote Fath al-Bari on Bukhari. Al-Nawawi, the compiler of yesterday's forty, wrote one on Sahih Muslim.
And the forties got commentaries of their own. So what does a commentator do? Take a line you already hold: actions are only by intentions.
He starts with the words. What is an intention, exactly? A passing thought, or a settled direction of the heart?

teach.h: FIRST THE WORDS, THEN THE CHAIN.
teach.b: Then the chain: who carried it, and from whom.
Then the rest of the text, because the hadith doesn't stop where the slogan does.

In its fuller versions in Bukhari it goes on: whoever emigrated for Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is for Allah and His Messenger, and whoever emigrated for something of this world, or to marry a woman, his emigration is for what he emigrated for.
Read whole, it's about one outward act carrying two very different inner journeys. Then the questions of practice: does an act of worship count without an intention behind it?
Here commentators lay out the views of earlier scholars, say who held them, and weigh them.

The saying sits in the center. The commentator stands around it, quoting others, disagreeing politely, admitting where he's unsure. The aim isn't to replace the Prophet's words but to keep them from being misread.
Ibn Hajar even asks why al-Bukhari opened his book with this report, and one answer given is that the author was setting his own intention right before the work began.

how: Students of hadith read a collection alongside a commentary, such as Ibn Hajar's Fath al-Bari on Bukhari or al-Nawawi's commentary on Muslim, usually with a teacher who explains the commentary in turn.

the saying stays in the center; the commentary opens it up around it.

games.q: you're writing a commentary. you reach a line whose meaning earlier scholars disagreed on. what do you write?
o: only the view you prefer, as if no other existed.
the views, who held them, and how you weigh them.
games.why: commentaries lay out the earlier views, name who held them, and then weigh them. the disagreement stays on the page.

practice: Take the line, actions are only by intentions, and pick one word from it: actions, or only, or intentions. Hold it the way a commentator would: what does it mean, and what would the line lose without it?
Then let the questions go and rest with the whole line on the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sharh. An explanation, a commentary written around a hadith collection, saying by saying, like Ibn Hajar's on Bukhari. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: explanation; the name for a commentary on a text.

carryVoice: Your line: explained for us. The saying stays in the center. Until tomorrow.
